conceptTag: Should a restaurant group buy its supplier?
readerTitle: Should twelve restaurants buy their own bakery?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 그룹과 베이커리, 철물 소매 체인과 유통업체, 배관 서비스 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 새 개념 없이 STR-09-02(진짜 시너지와 상상 속 시너지)와 STR-09-03(통합)을 적용하는 레슨
insight: 공급업체 인수는 '그들의 마진을 되찾는' 일이 아니다. 계약으로는 만들 수 없는 새 가치가 있는지, 그 가치만 건드리는 통합을 할 수 있는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 공급업체를 사면 그동안 내던 마진이 고스란히 내 이익이 된다. 사고 나면 우리 방식으로 합치는 것이 효율적이다.

sources.text: 기업전략의 표준 개념 (수직 통합, 시너지 평가, 인수 후 통합)
모든 기업과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 베이커리 연간 이익 $200,000 중 우리 주문에서 나오는 이익 $120,000(60%), 다른 고객에서 $80,000(40%). 인수 가격 $1.5M은 연간 이익의 7.5배(1,500,000 ÷ 200,000 = 7.5). 다시 확인이 필요합니다.
공동 발주 계획으로 줄어드는 폐기 비용 연 $60,000은 가상 가정입니다. 카드에서 '진짜 시너지'의 예로만 씁니다.
다른 고객(경쟁 카페)이 이탈하면 오븐 가동률이 떨어져 빵 한 개당 고정비가 오른다는 설명은 고정비 배분의 일반 원리로, 특정 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Should twelve restaurants buy their own bakery?
body: Maya runs twelve neighborhood restaurants. Every morning, one local bakery delivers all their bread and pastries.
The bakery's owner wants to retire and offers to sell for $1.5 million. Maya's first thought: *we've been paying their markup for years. Buy them, and that money stays with us.*
It's a common instinct. Let's test it with two ideas from this unit.

image.label: Bakery van delivering bread to a row of restaurants
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침, 작은 베이커리 밴 한 대가 같은 모양의 식당 여러 곳 앞을 지나며 빵 바구니를 내려놓는 장면. 밴 옆에 물음표가 붙은 가격표. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which benefit is real?
body: The bakery earns $200,000 a year in profit. About $120,000 of it comes from Maya's orders. The rest comes from other cafés in town.
Maya's team lists three reasons to buy. Which one is a benefit that only owning the bakery creates?

options.text: We stop paying their markup and keep the profit ourselves
options.feedback: This is an **imagined synergy**. The seller prices the bakery on its profit, including the profit from Maya's orders, so she pays for that markup up front.

options.text: We plan baking around our menus and cut waste across twelve kitchens
options.feedback: This is a **real synergy**: new value that neither business creates alone. It still needs to be measured, but it's money that doesn't exist today.

options.text: We keep selling to the bakery's other café customers
options.feedback: That income is worth having, but it isn't new. And some of those cafés compete with Maya. They may not want to buy bread from a rival.

cards.title: Money moving pockets isn't new money.
body: Before the deal, Maya pays the bakery's markup. After the deal, she owns that markup. But she paid $1.5 million for it, about 7.5 years of the bakery's profit.

The concept from **real vs imagined synergies** asks one question: what value exists *only* because the two are combined? Shared planning that cuts waste by, say, $60,000 a year passes that test. Keeping the markup doesn't.

image.label: Coins moving from one pocket to another in the same coat
image.brief: 한 외투의 왼쪽 주머니에서 오른쪽 주머니로 동전이 옮겨 가는 일러스트. 옆에 별도로 작은 새 동전 더미가 생기는 장면을 대비해 "Moved"와 "New" 라벨을 붙임.

cards.title: The bakery's other customers may leave.
body: About 40% of the bakery's profit comes from other cafés. Several of them compete with Maya's restaurants for the same lunch crowd.

Once Maya owns the bakery, those cafés may switch suppliers. Then the ovens and bakers sit idle part of the day, and each loaf carries more of the rent and wages. A lost synergy is as real as a gained one. Count both.

cards.title: Maya buys it. Now what?
body: The deal closes. The waste savings depend on bakery and kitchens planning together. The head baker has run the place for fifteen years.
How should Maya bring the bakery in?

options.text: Fold it into restaurant operations under her kitchen managers
options.feedback: Full **integration** looks tidy but puts baking under people who don't bake. If the head baker leaves, the quality Maya paid for may leave too.

options.text: Leave the bakery exactly as it was
options.feedback: This protects the people and the product, but nothing connects to the kitchens. The waste savings, the reason to buy, never happen.

options.text: Keep the bakery's team and customers, and link only order planning
options.feedback: Good **integration** joins only what creates the synergy and protects the rest. Here that means one shared ordering system, not a new boss.

cards.title: Owning a supplier removes your option to switch.
body: When you buy a supplier, you can't shop around if it falls behind on price or quality. A captive supplier also feels less pressure to improve.

Often a long-term contract with shared planning gets most of the real benefit without the purchase price. A plumbing firm can agree on stock levels with its parts wholesaler without buying it. Buy only when a contract can't deliver the value.
cards.softwareNote: A software company that buys a tool it depends on faces the same test. Owning the code helps only if it builds something together that a contract couldn't. Otherwise it just takes on another product to maintain.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store chain.
body: You run eight hardware stores. A regional distributor delivers most of your stock and is up for sale. Its other customers include independent shops that compete with you.
What question should you answer first?

options.text: How much markup do we pay them each year?
options.feedback: That's the markup illusion again. The seller will price that markup into the deal, so it isn't a gain.

options.text: What could we do as one company that a better contract couldn't?
options.feedback: This is the **real synergy** test, and it sets up the **integration** plan: join only the parts that create that value.

options.text: Will the distributor's key people stay after the sale?
options.feedback: A vital **integration** question, but it matters only once you know there's real value to protect.

cards.title: Buy a supplier for new value, not for its markup.
body: You used two ideas. **Real vs imagined synergies:** count only value that exists because you combine, and subtract the customers you might lose. **Integration:** join only what creates that value, and protect the people and customers you paid for.
**Try it today:** pick your biggest supplier. Write one thing you could do together if you owned it. Then ask whether a contract could do the same.
